quote: Kann man stets eine Fläche construiren, die eine vorgelegte Curve und nur diese zur Doppelcurve hat?
english: Can one always construct a surface that has a given curve, and only this curve, as its double curve?
topic: Hilbert notes the problem of bending a 2n-gon with identified sides into a regular surface, sketches the Boy surface, Klein bottle and ring surface as polygon identifications, proposes realizing Boy's surface algebraically, asks questions about surfaces with prescribed double curves and about embedding projective space in 4-space, and begins a remark on classifying partial differential equations by their characteristic equation.

triage.modern_statement: Given a curve C, is there always a surface whose double-point (self-intersection) locus is exactly C, with no other singular curve? There are two natural modern readings. (a) Algebraic: for a reduced space curve C in P^3, is there a surface S in P^3 whose 1-dimensional singular locus is exactly C, with S having ordinary double points along C (and perhaps pinch points and triple points), meaning S is singular along C and nowhere else along a curve? (b) Topological/differential: which curves or links in R^3, or which configurations of circles on the surface itself (the preimage of the double curve), can be the double-point set of a generic immersed or mapped closed surface?
triage.answered_by: No single source that settles this exact question was found. The topological reading has been answered in special cases in modern work. B. Kalmár (arXiv:1704.05823, 2017) characterizes which unions of disjoint embedded circles in the 2-sphere can be the multiple-point set of a generic immersion of the sphere into 3-space. The algebraic reading belongs to the classical theory of surfaces with ordinary singularities in P^3, where a double curve with pinch points and triple points is standard, for example as the double curve of a generic projection to P^3 of a smooth surface. However, no source retrieved here states an existence theorem for an arbitrary prescribed curve.

evidence.claim: Kalmár characterizes the unions of disjoint embedded circles in the 2-sphere that can be the multiple-point set of a generic immersion of the sphere into 3-space. This is a precise modern answer to the 'which curves are double curves' question for immersed spheres, stated on the source surface.

In modern algebraic geometry, surfaces in P^3 with ordinary singularities (a double curve as the singular locus, plus pinch points and triple points) are standard objects. They arise as the image of the double curve of a P^3 model, that is, a projection, of a surface in P^N.

Classical enumerative formulas for degree-n surfaces in P^3 with an ordinary double curve D, tau pinch points and t triple points are surveyed in a modern exposition. This shows that the double curve is a classical object of study.

The double curves of immersed surfaces in 3-space and their lifts to 4-space are an active topic. Immersed surfaces in 3-space have double curves and isolated triple points, and in general they are not projections of embedded surfaces in 4-space.
Double point curves of surface-knot diagrams, meaning projections of surfaces in 4-space to 3-space, are studied systematically in knot theory.

triage.why: This is a real research question, not a teaching or administrative note, and it sits on a page about Boy's surface and immersed or self-intersecting surfaces. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 published problems or the 24th problem. The general area of realizing double curves of surfaces is clearly studied today: Kalmár's 2017 characterization for immersed spheres, work on lifting immersed surfaces to 4-space, surface-knot diagrams, and classical formulas for surfaces with ordinary singularities. In the algebraic setting, I believe the question has a standard answer: for a smooth curve C in P^3, a general surface of high degree that is singular along C has C as its only double curve, by a Bertini-type argument. But I could not retrieve a source for that, so it is my own background knowledge and not established here. My search budget ran out before I could confirm it or find a historical answer from Hilbert's era. The 'solved' verdict is therefore tentative. A citable answer exists only for a specific topological version (spheres), not for Hilbert's general question as he phrased it.
